query: For Q235 steel in its pre-exposure state, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain the onset or suppression of corrosion-related degradation in harsh environments at room and elevated temperatures? Specify a controlled study that would isolate the governing cause, predicted observations relative to the untreated reference, applicable boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification result.

generation.hypothesis: A crack‐free high-entropy alloy (HEA) coating, specifically a CoCrFeNiMo0.85 deposited via laser metal deposition on Q235 steel, suppresses corrosion degradation in harsh environments by creating a continuous passive oxide barrier that minimizes the diffusion of corrosive species and prevents galvanic coupling between the coating and substrate. In contrast, coatings with manufacturing-induced microcracks promote local galvanic cells and accelerate corrosion.
generation.material_initial_state: Pre-exposure Q235 carbon steel with standard surface finish and microstructure.
generation.intervention: Deposition of a controlled CoCrFeNiMo0.85 HEA coating via laser metal deposition; comparison between an optimized, crack-free coating and a deliberately defect-introduced (microcracked) coating, alongside an untreated Q235 steel reference.
generation.conditions: Exposure in harsh corrosive environments, such as immersion in 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution at room temperature and under elevated temperature cycling that simulates geothermal conditions, to differentiate the thermal stress effects on coating integrity.
generation.structural_mediator: The structural integrity of the HEA coating—specifically the degree of cracking and porosity at the coating–substrate interface—which mediates the protective barrier effect and the likelihood of galvanic coupling with the underlying steel.
generation.mechanism: A continuous, defect-free HEA coating forms a stable passive oxide layer that inhibits corrosive ion ingress, effectively decoupling the substrate from the aggressive environment. Conversely, the presence of microcracks provides pathways for corrosive agents and establishes localized galvanic cells, accelerating the onset of pitting and corrosion on the Q235 substrate.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples with crack-free HEA coatings will exhibit significantly lower corrosion rates (e.g., reduced corrosion current density and mass loss) and fewer localized pits compared to both untreated Q235 steel and defect-laden HEA-coated samples, which should show enhanced localized corrosion and faster degradation.
generation.baseline: Untreated Q235 steel that, when exposed to the same harsh environments, experiences uniform corrosion and pitting corrosion at a predictable rate.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is applicable primarily to Q235 steel and to HEA coatings deposited by laser metal deposition under laboratory-controlled thermal conditions. Variability in deposition techniques, coating compositions, or environmental compositions may yield different behaviors.
generation.uncertainty: Quantitative differences among the treatments (e.g., the exact corrosion rate reduction) and the long-term stability of the HEA coatings under cyclic thermal stress require further investigation, as does the full impact of microstructural variations beyond visible cracks.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare three sets of Q235 steel samples: (a) untreated, (b) coated with CoCrFeNiMo0.85 HEA via optimized laser metal deposition parameters designed to yield crack-free coatings, and (c) coated with the same HEA but under modified conditions to deliberately introduce microcracks. Expose all samples to a 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution at room temperature and then to elevated temperature conditions simulating geothermal cycles. Evaluate corrosion performance over set time intervals.
measurements: Electrochemical measurements such as potentiodynamic polarization to determine corrosion current density and pitting potentials.
Surface and cross-sectional imaging (optical microscopy/SEM) to assess crack density, pit formation, and coating integrity.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the crack-free HEA coated samples do not exhibit significantly reduced corrosion (i.e., lower corrosion current density, less mass loss, and fewer or shallower pits) compared to the untreated steel, or if the defect-induced coatings do not demonstrate accelerated localized corrosion relative to the optimized coatings, then the proposed mechanism attributing corrosion suppression to barrier effects and the prevention of galvanic coupling is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In this paper, the CoCrFeNiTix HEA coatings are prepared on Q235 steel substrate by laser cladding. The effect of Ti content on the microstructure and corrosion resistance in a 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution was studied. Furthermore, the corrosion resistance mechanism was analyzed experimentally and by first-principles calculations.

In our study, two high-entropy coatings were tested in three different geothermal environments. High-entropy alloy (HEA) coatings of CoCrFeNiMo0.85 (Mo-HEA) were deposited using laser metal deposition (LMD) onto carbon steel (S235JR) and stainless steel (316L) substrates, and Al0.5CoCrFeNi (Al-HEA) coating was deposited using LMD onto stainless steel (304L) substrate. Erosion and corrosion resistance performance of the systems was evaluated after exposure in three different environments at the Helliseidi geothermal power plant: wellhead, aerated, and erosion test. In-depth metallographic examination and optical profilometry were performed to obtain information on the erosion damage and growth of the corrosive scale. The research has highlighted the following main findings: The LMD CoCrFeNiMo0.85 coating was prone to manufacturing cracking, in some cases throughout the coating, when deposited on carbon steel substrate, but not on stainless steel. Wide manufacturing cracks are concluded to enhance the fluid-induced erosion effect for the CoCrFeNiMo0.85 coating in the vicinity of the cracks. From our results, it is concluded that LMD-manufactured CoCrFeNiMo0.85 coating could be a promising erosion- and corrosion-resistant coating candidate on less erosion-corrosion-resistant materials for application in geothermal environments. The formulation and production of the CoCrFeNiMo0.85 coating, however, need to be further optimized to prevent cracking of the CoCrFeNiMo0.85 coating on a carbon steel substrate. It is concluded that an Al0.5CoCrFeNi coating is not suitable for application as a coating material in a geothermal environment.

chosen.approach: HEA coating deposition on Q235 (carbon) steel via thermal methods
